text: The principle of (weak) mathematical induction proves ∀n ∈ ℕ, P(n) by establishing which two things?
choices: P(n) for one arbitrary n, and P(n+1) unconditionally
That the set {n : ¬P(n)} is infinite, then a contradiction
The base case P(0), and the inductive step ∀n (P(n) → P(n+1))
explanation: Weak induction needs a base case P(0) and an inductive step showing P(n) → P(n+1) for every n; together they yield ∀n P(n). Proving only P(0) and P(1) covers just two values; the inductive step is conditional (you assume P(n)), not unconditional; and option C describes a different, minimal-counterexample style of argument.
